display_name: Lafage, Côtes Catalanes Vieilles Vignes Tessellae
raw_content:
{
  "hook": "This bottle proves the IGP Côtes Catalanes designation can outperform many AOC neighbors at half the price. Old vines across the Roussillon landscape converge in this blend, leveraging schist and gneiss soils to build density without heavy extraction. Jean-Marc Lafage sources fruit from 118 communes within the Pyrénées-Orientales, ensuring consistency despite vintage variation.",
  "wine_summary": "Operating as a négociant-éleveur with his own holdings, Jean-Marc Lafage focuses on volume and value rather than single-vineyard exclusivity. Tessellae represents the core of this operation, blending Syrah, Carignan, Grenache, and Mourvèdre to capture the sun-baked character of the Mediterranean climate. The Tramontane wind strips humidity from the vines, concentrating sugars and phenolics while preventing rot, which explains the reliable ripeness across vintages like 2012 and 2014.",
  "terroir_expression": "Across the Pyrénées-Orientales, schist and gneiss dominate the subsoil in many of the sourced parcels, forcing roots deep for water and imparting a stony mineral edge to the fruit. High altitude plots in the foothills of the Pyrenees retain acidity better than the coastal plains, balancing the 14.5% alcohol potential. Heat accumulation during the day followed by rapid cooling at night preserves fresh dark fruit characters against the baked earth notes typical of the region.",
  "vinification_summary": "To preserve primary fruit aromas, fermentation occurs in temperature-controlled stainless steel tanks before aging in concrete vats or large oak foudres. This approach avoids the vanilla and toast notes associated with new barriques, letting the Carignan's savory iron and olive characteristics shine through. Minimal intervention during élevage ensures the tannic structure remains firm but accessible upon release.",
  "food_pairing": "Pair with lamb shoulder braised with olives and rosemary to match the wine's savory herb notes while tannins cut the fat. Nashville hot chicken works well because the fruit sweetness offsets the heat and the acidity cleanses the palate. Grilled sardines with romesco provide a smoky char that matches the wine's earthy depth. Hard aged cheeses like Manchego stand up to the alcohol weight.",
  "comparable_wines": "Mas Amiel Côtes du Roussillon Villages — similar old-vine Carignan focus but often stricter appellation rules. Domaine Gauby 2004 — higher price point but same regional profile. Les Vignerons de la Domitienne Corbières — another high-value Languedoc-Roussillon blend.",
  "style_profile": "Full-bodied dry red with firm tannins and earthy depth",
  "cellar_recommendation": "Storage requires a cool dark place at 55°F if holding beyond six months. Drink now through 2026 to catch the primary fruit before tertiary earth takes over.",
  "value_assessment": "$15 places this in the everyday drinking category, undercutting most Roussillon AOCs by $10 or more. Competitors like Les Vignerons de la Domitienne offer similar volume but lack the old-vine concentration found here. The price-to-quality ratio is unmatched for blended Southern French reds.",
  "market_position": "You will find this on retail shelves, appearing in independent shops and larger chains like LCBO. Restaurants seeking high-margin by-the-glass options utilize this for its consistency and recognizable regional style. Casual drinkers buying for weeknight dinners form the core audience.",
  "insider_take": "Delicate Pinot Noir drinkers should skip this, as the alcohol and extract demand robust food. The tradeoff for the low price is lack of vineyard specificity, but the blend compensates with reliability. Buy by the case for winter meals rather than special occasions.",

parsed.hook: This bottle proves the IGP Côtes Catalanes designation can outperform many AOC neighbors at half the price. Old vines across the Roussillon landscape converge in this blend, leveraging schist and gneiss soils to build density without heavy extraction. Jean-Marc Lafage sources fruit from 118 communes within the Pyrénées-Orientales, ensuring consistency despite vintage variation.
parsed.wine_summary: Operating as a négociant-éleveur with his own holdings, Jean-Marc Lafage focuses on volume and value rather than single-vineyard exclusivity. Tessellae represents the core of this operation, blending Syrah, Carignan, Grenache, and Mourvèdre to capture the sun-baked character of the Mediterranean climate. The Tramontane wind strips humidity from the vines, concentrating sugars and phenolics while preventing rot, which explains the reliable ripeness across vintages like 2012 and 2014.
parsed.terroir_expression: Across the Pyrénées-Orientales, schist and gneiss dominate the subsoil in many of the sourced parcels, forcing roots deep for water and imparting a stony mineral edge to the fruit. High altitude plots in the foothills of the Pyrenees retain acidity better than the coastal plains, balancing the 14.5% alcohol potential. Heat accumulation during the day followed by rapid cooling at night preserves fresh dark fruit characters against the baked earth notes typical of the region.
parsed.vinification_summary: To preserve primary fruit aromas, fermentation occurs in temperature-controlled stainless steel tanks before aging in concrete vats or large oak foudres. This approach avoids the vanilla and toast notes associated with new barriques, letting the Carignan's savory iron and olive characteristics shine through. Minimal intervention during élevage ensures the tannic structure remains firm but accessible upon release.
parsed.food_pairing: Pair with lamb shoulder braised with olives and rosemary to match the wine's savory herb notes while tannins cut the fat. Nashville hot chicken works well because the fruit sweetness offsets the heat and the acidity cleanses the palate. Grilled sardines with romesco provide a smoky char that matches the wine's earthy depth. Hard aged cheeses like Manchego stand up to the alcohol weight.
parsed.comparable_wines: Mas Amiel Côtes du Roussillon Villages — similar old-vine Carignan focus but often stricter appellation rules. Domaine Gauby 2004 — higher price point but same regional profile. Les Vignerons de la Domitienne Corbières — another high-value Languedoc-Roussillon blend.
parsed.style_profile: Full-bodied dry red with firm tannins and earthy depth
parsed.cellar_recommendation: Storage requires a cool dark place at 55°F if holding beyond six months. Drink now through 2026 to catch the primary fruit before tertiary earth takes over.
parsed.value_assessment: $15 places this in the everyday drinking category, undercutting most Roussillon AOCs by $10 or more. Competitors like Les Vignerons de la Domitienne offer similar volume but lack the old-vine concentration found here. The price-to-quality ratio is unmatched for blended Southern French reds.
parsed.market_position: You will find this on retail shelves, appearing in independent shops and larger chains like LCBO. Restaurants seeking high-margin by-the-glass options utilize this for its consistency and recognizable regional style. Casual drinkers buying for weeknight dinners form the core audience.
parsed.insider_take: Delicate Pinot Noir drinkers should skip this, as the alcohol and extract demand robust food. The tradeoff for the low price is lack of vineyard specificity, but the blend compensates with reliability. Buy by the case for winter meals rather than special occasions.
